# Purpose and precise meaning of equivalence

This note assumes that the reader already understands the construction in
the `main` branch of NAFDEMG and the numerical experiments in `main.tex`:
assemble finite element matrices, project the initial condition, assemble
the forcing, apply the rational backward Euler update, and measure the
error on a reference space--time mesh. It derives the construction used by
NAP and `main_copy.tex` from those objects.

The central statement is conditional and exact:

> Fix the same actual uniform graph mesh, time grid, physical data, and
> scalar rational function. Assemble the initial and forcing loads exactly.
> Then the matrix update and NAP's modal recurrence produce the same finite
> element function at every solver time. The modal formula for its spatial
> error is also exact in real arithmetic.

Several additional choices must be distinguished from this identity.
NAP uses exact spatial loads, a different source of rational coefficients,
different experiment parameters, and a different quadrature for the
space--time error. Thus equivalence of the discrete evolution does not mean
equality of the numbers produced by the two repositories with their shipped
settings.

The note separates four mathematical objects throughout:

| Object | Meaning |
|---|---|
| The continuum solution \(u\) | The solution of the differential equation |
| The discrete iterates \(U_{h,m}^k\) | The rational FEM/backward Euler solution |
| The exact error \(E\) | The norm of the difference between those two functions, with right-constant time reconstruction |
| The reported errors \(E_\star\) and \(\widehat E\) | Different quadrature approximations to that norm |

All equations needed for the comparison are written here. No paper equation
numbers or source line numbers are needed. The comparison of settings uses
the NAFDEMG `main` sources at commit
`bdbfc925d1ccc92d7378f45d7ed9c86d765e9656` and the NAP sources inspected on
the date above. The final source guide links the relevant files. This
document contains no executable experiment chunks and has no dependency on
saved error matrices or notification services.

# Start from the familiar matrix construction

## The model, finite element space, and coefficient vectors

Let \(\Gamma\) be the tadpole with a terminal edge of length 1 and a loop
of length 2. Define

\[
L=\kappa^2-\Delta_\Gamma,\qquad \beta=\alpha/2,\qquad
\partial_tu+L^\beta u=f,\qquad u(0)=u_0.
\]

The domain of the Kirchhoff--Laplacian imposes continuity at vertices and
zero sum of outgoing derivatives. At the degree-one terminal vertex this
is a Neumann condition.

Take the same continuous P1 finite element space \(V_h\) as in the matrix
construction, with nodal basis \(\{\psi_i\}_{i=1}^{N_h}\). Write

\[
v_h=\sum_i V_i\psi_i,\qquad
C_{ij}=(\psi_j,\psi_i),\qquad
G_{ij}=(\psi_j',\psi_i'),\qquad K=\kappa^2C+G.
\]

Inner products without a subscript are in \(L_2(\Gamma)\). The coefficient
vector \(V\) and the function \(v_h\) are different representations of
the same finite element object. In particular,

\[
\|v_h\|^2=V^{\mathsf T}CV.
\]

The discrete operator is defined by

\[
(L_hv_h,z_h)=\kappa^2(v_h,z_h)+(v_h',z_h')
\quad\text{for every }z_h\in V_h.
\]

Its coefficient matrix is \(C^{-1}K\). The matrix named `L` in the
NAFDEMG convergence notebooks is \(K\), not \(C^{-1}K\). Accordingly,
discrete eigenvectors satisfy the generalized eigenproblem

\[
KV=\lambda_h CV.
\]

This distinction is important when translating the shifted solves in the
old code into scalar eigenvalue formulas.

## Projection and loads

The orthogonal projection \(P_hv\in V_h\) is characterized by

\[
(P_hv,z_h)=(v,z_h)\quad\text{for every }z_h\in V_h.
\]

If \(b(v)_i=(v,\psi_i)\), its coefficient vector is
\(C^{-1}b(v)\). Thus the familiar initialization

\[
CU^0=b(u_0)
\]

already gives \(P_hu_0\). No change from nodal initialization to
orthogonal initialization is involved in moving to NAP.

For uniform times \(t_k=k\tau\), \(N\tau=T\), the forcing average is

\[
f^k=\frac1\tau\int_{t_{k-1}}^{t_k}f(t)\,dt,
\qquad F_i^k=(f^k,\psi_i).
\]

The coefficient vector of \(P_hf^k\) is \(C^{-1}F^k\).
For \(\beta=1\), the usual backward Euler update is

\[
(C+\tau K)U^k=CU^{k-1}+\tau F^k.
\]

The fractional/rational update replaces \(L_h\) by an approximation of
\(L_h^\beta\), while retaining the same mass inner product and loads.

## The exact solution is already a two-mode solution

For orthonormal continuum eigenfunctions \(Le_j=\lambda_je_j\), the
benchmark data are

\[
u_0=10e_5,\qquad f(t)=10\sin(\pi t)e_7,\qquad
w_5=3\pi/2,\quad w_7=2\pi,\quad \lambda_j=\kappa^2+w_j^2.
\]

Set \(a_j=\lambda_j^\beta\). Both manuscripts use

\[
u(t)=c_5(t)e_5+c_7(t)e_7,
\]

\[
c_5(t)=10e^{-a_5t},\qquad
c_7(t)=\frac{10}{a_7^2+\pi^2}
\left[a_7\sin(\pi t)-\pi\cos(\pi t)+\pi e^{-a_7t}\right].
\]

This is the full continuum solution for these data. Taking only these
two modes introduces no spectral truncation error. A new fact must still
be proved before reducing the *discrete* solution to two modes: the
projections of these functions must span an invariant subspace of the
discrete operator. That is the purpose of the next section.

# Why the projected modes are discrete eigenfunctions

## The extra mesh assumption

NAP chooses a single element length \(h=1/n\). The terminal edge has
\(n\) elements and the loop has \(2n\) elements. Every element on both
edges therefore has exactly the same length.

For a requested target \(\eta\), NAP uses

\[
n=\max\{1,\lceil\eta^{-1}\rceil\},\qquad h=1/n,
\]

with a floating-point snap near integer reciprocals. The following proof
concerns the actual partition. Two mesh generators receiving the same
target need not produce the same partition; a comparison must match the
actual element lengths and connectivity.

Let \(I_he\) be the nodal interpolant of a continuum eigenfunction with
wave number \(w\), so \(-e''=w^2e\) on every edge. Its nodal coefficient
vector is \(E_v=e(v)\). We first prove that \(I_he\) is a discrete
eigenfunction, and then identify \(P_he\).

## The vertex conditions preserve the trigonometric stencil

At any mesh node \(v\), parameterize each incident element by distance
\(s\) directed away from the node. Let \(d_v\) count the incident
elements, counting the two ends of a loop separately. On incidence \(r\),

\[
e_r(s)=E_v\cos(ws)+\frac{\partial_re(v)}{w}\sin(ws).
\]

Write \(z=wh\). Summing the values at the neighboring nodes gives

\[
\sum_{r=1}^{d_v}e_r(h)
=d_v E_v\cos z+
\frac{\sin z}{w}\sum_{r=1}^{d_v}\partial_re(v)
=d_v E_v\cos z.
\]

The derivative sum vanishes at graph vertices by the Kirchhoff condition.
At an interior edge node the two outgoing derivatives cancel by smoothness.
At the terminal vertex its single outgoing derivative is zero. Thus this
identity covers the degree-three junction as well as ordinary edge nodes.

For P1 elements, each incident element contributes
\((E_v-E_{\mathrm{neighbor}})/h\) to the stiffness row and
\(h(2E_v+E_{\mathrm{neighbor}})/6\) to the mass row. Hence

\[
(GE)_v=\frac{d_v}{h}(1-\cos z)E_v,
\qquad
(CE)_v=\frac{d_vh}{6}(2+\cos z)E_v.
\]

Their ratio is independent of the node and its degree:

\[
GE=\nu_h(w)CE,\qquad
\nu_h(w)=\frac{6(1-\cos(wh))}{h^2(2+\cos(wh))}
=\frac{12\sin^2(wh/2)}{h^2(2+\cos(wh))}.
\]

Adding the shift yields

\[
KE=\lambda_h(w)CE,\qquad
\lambda_h(w)=\kappa^2+\nu_h(w).
\]

This establishes the eigenfunction property for the interpolant. Equal
element lengths make the same trigonometric factor appear in every row.

## The projection is a scalar multiple of the interpolant

Let \(b_i=(e,\psi_i)\), and let \(p\) be the coefficients of \(P_he\),
so \(Cp=b\). On each element the derivative of any \(v_h\in V_h\) is
constant. The fundamental theorem of calculus therefore gives

\[
\big((I_he)',v_h'\big)
=\sum_{[a,b]}v_h'|_{[a,b]}\,[e(b)-e(a)]
=(e',v_h').
\]

Integration by parts on all edges and cancellation of the vertex terms give

\[
(e',v_h')=w^2(e,v_h).
\]

Taking nodal test functions yields \(GE=w^2b\). Combining this with
\(GE=\nu_h(w)CE\), for \(w>0\), gives

\[
p=C^{-1}b=\rho_h(w)E,\qquad
\rho_h(w)=\frac{\nu_h(w)}{w^2}
=\frac{3\operatorname{sinc}^2(wh/2)}{2+\cos(wh)},
\]

where \(\operatorname{sinc}(x)=\sin(x)/x\), continuously extended by
\(\operatorname{sinc}(0)=1\). Thus

\[
\boxed{P_he=\rho_h(w)I_he,\qquad
L_hP_he=\lambda_h(w)P_he.}
\]

For \(w=0\), the eigenfunction is constant and belongs to \(V_h\), so
the same statement holds with \(\rho_h(0)=1\) and
\(\lambda_h(0)=\kappa^2\).

The proportionality factor matters: projection and interpolation are
different functions in general. NAP uses the projected functions. The
proof is an identity of this uniform P1 setting and does not assert that
orthogonal projection generally preserves continuum eigenfunctions on
arbitrary meshes.

For the modes retained by NAP, \(0<wh<\pi/2\). This resolution condition
keeps the sampled modes nonzero and away from aliasing. The formula also
shows that the FEM eigenvalue is genuinely different from the continuum
one:

\[
\lambda_h(w)=\kappa^2+w^2+\frac{w^4h^2}{12}+O(h^4)
\quad\text{for fixed }w.
\]

## An explicit check at the tadpole junction

Choose terminal-edge coordinate \(x\in[0,1]\), directed toward the
junction, and loop coordinate \(x\in[0,2]\), beginning and ending there.
The two normalized modes can be written

\[
e_5|_{\mathrm{terminal}}=\frac2{\sqrt3}\cos(3\pi x/2),
\qquad
e_5|_{\mathrm{loop}}=\frac1{\sqrt3}\sin(3\pi x/2),
\]

\[
e_7|_{\mathrm{terminal}}=\sqrt{\frac23}\cos(2\pi x),
\qquad
e_7|_{\mathrm{loop}}=\sqrt{\frac23}\cos(2\pi x).
\]

For \(e_5\), the three outgoing derivatives at the junction are
\(-2w_5/\sqrt3\), \(w_5/\sqrt3\), and \(w_5/\sqrt3\), whose sum
vanishes. For \(e_7\), all three derivatives vanish individually.
These are concrete instances of the cancellation used in the matrix proof.

# Where the projection norm and orthogonality formulas come from

## Deriving the scalar weight \(g_{j,h}\)

The projected modes \(\phi_{j,h}=P_he_j\) need not have unit norm. NAP
retains their squared norms rather than renormalizing their coefficients.
We now derive the weight used in its error formula.

Define a diagonal matrix \(D_h\) by
\((D_h)_{vv}=d_vh/2\). Its quadratic form is the composite trapezoidal
sum of nodal squares. The mass-row formula above implies

\[
CE=\frac{2+\cos z}{3}D_hE.
\]

For either of the two normalized modes displayed above,

\[
E^{\mathsf T}D_hE=1.
\]

Indeed, their squares are linear combinations of constants and
\(\cos(2wx)\) on each edge. For these edge lengths and frequencies, the
integral and the uniform composite trapezoidal sum of each oscillatory
term both vanish. This can be checked by summing a geometric progression.
Consequently the trapezoidal sum equals the exact normalized squared norm.
The resolution condition excludes the aliasing cases of that sum.

It follows that

\[
\|I_he_j\|^2=E_j^{\mathsf T}CE_j=\frac{2+\cos z_j}{3},
\qquad z_j=w_jh.
\]

Since \(P_he_j=\rho_h(w_j)I_he_j\),

\[
\boxed{
g_{j,h}:=\|P_he_j\|^2
=\rho_h(w_j)^2\frac{2+\cos z_j}{3}
=\frac{3\operatorname{sinc}^4(z_j/2)}{2+\cos z_j}.}
\]

The diagonal matrix \(D_h\) was used only to prove the identity. The
evolution scheme and the projection still use the consistent mass matrix
\(C\).

## Why there are no cross terms for modes 5 and 7

The operator \(L_h\) is self-adjoint in the mass inner product. Thus

\[
\lambda_{5,h}(\phi_{5,h},\phi_{7,h})
=(L_h\phi_{5,h},\phi_{7,h})
=(\phi_{5,h},L_h\phi_{7,h})
=\lambda_{7,h}(\phi_{5,h},\phi_{7,h}).
\]

The function \(\nu_h(w)\) is strictly increasing for \(0<wh<\pi\),
so the two resolved wave numbers have distinct discrete eigenvalues.
Therefore \((\phi_{5,h},\phi_{7,h})=0\).

Projection orthogonality also gives

\[
(e_i-P_he_i,e_j-P_he_j)
=\delta_{ij}-(P_he_i,P_he_j).
\]

The residual modes are consequently orthogonal as well, with squared
norms \(1-g_{j,h}\). In particular,

\[
1-g_{j,h}=\frac{z_j^4}{720}+O(z_j^6),\qquad
\|e_j-P_he_j\|=O(h^2).
\]

The small projection error is fully present even though no reference mesh
is constructed.

# The rational matrix update becomes the same scalar multiplier

## Keep the inverse approximation and the decay rate distinct

Introduce the normalized coefficient operator

\[
B=\kappa^{-2}C^{-1}K.
\]

Its eigenvalues are \(z_j=\lambda_{j,h}/\kappa^2\), not
\(\lambda_{j,h}\) themselves. Given polynomials

\[
q_1(x)=c_m\prod_{i=1}^m(x-\xi_i),\qquad
q_2(x)=b_{m+1}\prod_{i=1}^{m+1}(x-\zeta_i),
\]

approximate \(x^{\beta-1}\) by \(q_1(x)/q_2(x)\). Multiplication by
\(x\), followed by \(x=z^{-1}\), gives

\[
\mathcal R_{m,\beta}(z)
=x\frac{q_1(x)}{q_2(x)}\bigg|_{x=1/z}
=F_{m,\beta}\frac{P(z)}{Q(z)}\approx z^{-\beta},
\]

\[
F_{m,\beta}=\frac{c_m}{b_{m+1}},\qquad
P(z)=\prod_{i=1}^m(1-\xi_i z),\qquad
Q(z)=\prod_{i=1}^{m+1}(1-\zeta_i z).
\]

The list fields `pr_roots`, `pl_roots`, and `factor` store
\(\xi_i\), \(\zeta_i\), and \(F_{m,\beta}\), respectively. The
stored roots are roots in the reciprocal variable \(x\); the poles of
\(\mathcal R\) as a function of \(z\) are \(1/\zeta_i\).

Let \(\mathcal R(B)\) denote the resulting matrix function. The
approximation of \(L_h^\beta\) is represented by

\[
A_{h,m}=\kappa^{2\beta}\mathcal R(B)^{-1}.
\]

Thus \(\mathcal R\) approximates an inverse power, whereas the positive
decay rate involves its reciprocal. These two roles explain the division
in NAP's `rational_modal_rates()`.

## Recovering the original shifted solves

For \(q^k=U^{k-1}+\tau C^{-1}F^k\), the rational backward Euler update is

\[
U^k=S_\tau(B)q^k,\qquad
S_\tau(z)=\frac{\mathcal R(z)}{\mathcal R(z)+\tau\kappa^{2\beta}}
=\frac{P(z)}{P(z)+\sigma Q(z)},\qquad
\sigma=\frac{\tau\kappa^{2\beta}}{F_{m,\beta}}.
\]

If \(p_\ell\) are the simple poles of this update, its partial fraction
representation is

\[
S_\tau(z)=\sum_{\ell=1}^{m+1}\frac{r_\ell}{z-p_\ell}.
\]

Since

\[
B-p_\ell I=C^{-1}(K/\kappa^2-p_\ell C),
\]

we obtain exactly the matrix form used by the original solver:

\[
\boxed{
U^k=\sum_{\ell=1}^{m+1}r_\ell
(K/\kappa^2-p_\ell C)^{-1}
(CU^{k-1}+\tau F^k).}
\]

For simple poles the residue can be written in either form

\[
r_\ell=
\frac{P(p_\ell)}{P'(p_\ell)+\sigma Q'(p_\ell)}
=-\frac{\sigma Q(p_\ell)}{P'(p_\ell)+\sigma Q'(p_\ell)}.
\]

Their equality follows from the pole equation
\(P(p_\ell)+\sigma Q(p_\ell)=0\). The second form is the stable
residue expression discussed in `main_copy.tex`. NAP's minimal modal
runtime does not form these poles or residues; they explain its relationship
to a sparse implementation.

## Evaluating that same update on a projected mode

Let \(p_j\) be the nodal coefficient vector of \(\phi_{j,h}\). Then

\[
Bp_j=\frac{\lambda_{j,h}}{\kappa^2}p_j,
\qquad
A_{h,m}p_j=\widehat a_{j,h,m}p_j,
\]

\[
\widehat a_{j,h,m}
=\frac{\kappa^{2\beta}}
{\mathcal R_{m,\beta}(\lambda_{j,h}/\kappa^2)},\qquad
S_\tau(B)p_j=\mu_jp_j,\qquad
\mu_j=(1+\tau\widehat a_{j,h,m})^{-1}.
\]

This is an application of the same rational function to an eigenvector.
All matrix dimensions and mass factors remain accounted for in the
generalized eigenvalue relation.

Finite negative roots and a positive factor make \(\mathcal R(z)>0\)
for \(z>0\). Hence \(\widehat a_j>0\), \(0<\mu_j<1\), and the update
is a contraction in the \(C\)-inner product. The implicit update is
uniquely defined. These facts will justify the invariant-subspace argument.

# Exact loads and the two-dimensional invariant subspace

## Which part of the old assembly changes

Write

\[
u_0=\sum_{j\in\{5,7\}}x_je_j,\qquad
f(t)=A\sin(\omega t)\sum_{j\in\{5,7\}}y_je_j,
\]

where the benchmark has \(x=(10,0)\), \(y=(0,10)\), \(A=1\),
and \(\omega=\pi\). Define exact load vectors
\((b_j)_i=(e_j,\psi_i)\), so \(b_j=Cp_j\).

The initial vector is

\[
U^0=C^{-1}\sum_jx_jb_j=\sum_jx_jp_j.
\]

This agrees with the analytic initial projection in NAFDEMG-main.
For the forcing, however, NAFDEMG-main uses

\[
\widetilde b_7=\Psi^{\mathsf T}C^\star e_7^\star\approx b_7.
\]

The reference mass matrix computes the inner product of the reference
piecewise linear interpolants of the sampled functions. This is an
approximation of the exact load, including when the continuum eigenfunction
itself is known analytically. NAP uses \(b_7\) exactly through its modal
projection formulas.

Thus exact equivalence is with the original matrix scheme *using exact
spatial loads*. The shipped reference-load assembly is a further
approximation of that scheme. If the reference partition is not nested in
the solver partition, its load approximation can also reflect interpolation
of the coarse hat functions onto the reference partition.

## Deriving the common time average

Let \(\theta=\omega\tau\). Direct integration gives

\[
\overline g_k=\frac1\tau\int_{(k-1)\tau}^{k\tau}A\sin(\omega t)\,dt
=A\operatorname{sinc}(\theta/2)\sin((k-\tfrac12)\theta).
\]

For \(\omega\ne0\), this equals
\(A[\cos((k-1)\theta)-\cos(k\theta)]/(\omega\tau)\).
The sinc form preserves the small-step limit accurately. Both constructions
use interval averages, and the load vector is

\[
F^k=\overline g_k\sum_jy_jb_j,
\qquad C^{-1}F^k=\overline g_k\sum_jy_jp_j.
\]

## Why no other discrete modes are required

Set \(\mathcal W_h=\operatorname{span}\{\phi_{5,h},\phi_{7,h}\}\).
The initial condition belongs to \(\mathcal W_h\), every projected forcing
average belongs to \(\mathcal W_h\), and \(S_\tau(L_h/\kappa^2)\)
maps each basis function of \(\mathcal W_h\) to a scalar multiple of
itself. Therefore every iterate remains in \(\mathcal W_h\).

In detail, if \(U_{h,m}^{k-1}=\sum_jb_j^{k-1}\phi_{j,h}\), then the
matrix update derived above gives

\[
U_{h,m}^k=\sum_j\mu_j
\left(b_j^{k-1}+\tau y_j\overline g_k\right)\phi_{j,h}.
\]

Thus its coefficients satisfy

\[
\boxed{b_j^0=x_j,\qquad
b_j^k=\mu_j(b_j^{k-1}+\tau y_j\overline g_k).}
\]

Induction and uniqueness establish equality with the full matrix solution
for every integer step. All coefficients in the complementary discrete
eigenspaces are zero. The full finite element space is still present in
the definition of the scheme; these particular data simply excite an
invariant two-dimensional subspace.

## What a reference-load discrepancy does

With \(\widetilde b_7\) in place of \(b_7\), the projected forcing is
perturbed by the finite element function whose vector is

\[
\delta q=10C^{-1}(\widetilde b_7-b_7).
\]

For identical other inputs and \(A=1\), the difference \(D^k\) between
the two coefficient solutions satisfies

\[
D^0=0,\qquad D^k=S_\tau(B)
\left(D^{k-1}+\tau\overline g_k\delta q\right).
\]

Here \(\overline g_k\) is the average of \(\sin(\omega t)\), with
the factor 10 already included in \(\delta q\). Contractivity implies

\[
\|D^k\|_C\leq\tau\sum_{\ell=1}^k|\overline g_\ell|\,\|\delta q\|_C
\leq T\|\delta q\|_C.
\]

This explains mathematically how an approximate load changes the result
and how its effect disappears as the load approximation converges. A
general load perturbation need not lie in \(\mathcal W_h\).

# Closed evaluation of the backward Euler recurrence

## Summing the recurrence, rather than advancing it

For one mode, write \(\mu=(1+\tau\widehat a)^{-1}\), initial coefficient
\(x\), and forcing coefficient \(y\). Repeated substitution gives

\[
b^k=\mu^kx+\tau\mu y\sum_{\ell=1}^k\mu^{k-\ell}\overline g_\ell.
\]

The trigonometric average has the complex representation

\[
\overline g_\ell=A\operatorname{sinc}(\theta/2)
\operatorname{Im}\left(e^{i(\ell-1/2)\theta}\right),
\qquad\theta=\omega\tau.
\]

The geometric progression is

\[
\sum_{\ell=1}^k\mu^{k-\ell}e^{i(\ell-1/2)\theta}
=e^{i\theta/2}\frac{e^{ik\theta}-\mu^k}{e^{i\theta}-\mu}.
\]

Hence the closed solution is

\[
\boxed{
b^k=\mu^kx+
\tau\mu A y\operatorname{sinc}(\theta/2)
\operatorname{Im}\left[
e^{i\theta/2}\frac{e^{ik\theta}-\mu^k}{e^{i\theta}-\mu}
\right].}
\]

At integer \(k\), this is exactly the result of \(k\) backward Euler
updates with interval-averaged forcing. No new time discretization has
been introduced. The denominator is nonzero because \(0<\mu<1\) and
\(|e^{i\theta}|=1\).

The formula requires only the step index \(k\), the scalar \(\tau\),
and the rate. For \(T=1\) and \(\tau=10^{-10}\), \(N=10^{10}\)
steps are defined mathematically, but a coefficient at step \(N\) is
obtained without computing the preceding iterates or storing their times.
NAFDEMG-main's streamed solver also saves memory compared with a full
solution matrix, but still traverses the solver steps needed by its
reference samples. These are different computational costs for the same
underlying recurrence when the inputs match.

## Three different rates remain distinct

The three relevant decay rates are

\[
a_j=(\kappa^2+w_j^2)^\beta,\qquad
a_{j,h}=\lambda_{j,h}^\beta,\qquad
\widehat a_{j,h,m}
=\frac{\kappa^{2\beta}}
{\mathcal R_{m,\beta}(\lambda_{j,h}/\kappa^2)}.
\]

They describe, respectively, continuum evolution, exact fractional FEM
evolution, and rational FEM evolution. Backward Euler then contributes
\(\mu_j=(1+\tau\widehat a_{j,h,m})^{-1}\).

Even if the rational approximation were exact, the numerical initial-data
decay would be \((1+\tau a_{j,h})^{-k}\), rather than
\(e^{-a_jk\tau}\). Both spatial and temporal discretization errors remain
in the closed formula.

When NAP's optional `diffusion` parameter is \(D>0\), all three rates
are multiplied by \(D\); the physical forcing is still the prescribed
\(A\sin(\omega t)\sum_jy_je_j\). The compared experiments use \(D=1\).
There is no forcing rescaling hidden in the acceleration.

# Replacing the reference spatial mesh by an exact error identity

## What the reference matrix measures

The original procedure evaluates the exact solution at reference nodes,
evaluates the numerical finite element function there through \(\Psi\),
and forms

\[
d_\ell=u^\star(t_\ell^\star)-\Psi U^{k(\ell)},\qquad
t_\ell^\star\in(t_{k(\ell)-1},t_{k(\ell)}],
\]

\[
E_\star^2=\tau_\star\sum_{\ell=1}^{N_\star}
d_\ell^{\mathsf T}C^\star d_\ell.
\]

The quadratic form is the exact squared norm of the *reference P1
interpolant of the nodal difference*. It approximates the spatial norm of
the continuum-minus-FEM difference. The right-endpoint time sum approximates
its integral in time. These approximations are present even though the
continuum solution can be evaluated analytically.

For a fixed numerical solution, refinement of the reference space and time
partitions targets its actual space--time error. In the old workflow,
refining \(h_\star\) can additionally change the numerical solution because
the same reference mesh is used to approximate the forcing load.

## Orthogonal decomposition of the full spatial error

Keep exactly the same right-constant reconstruction:

\[
U_{h,m}^\tau(t)=U_{h,m}^k\quad\text{for }t\in(t_{k-1},t_k].
\]

At a fixed time in that interval,

\[
u(t)-U_{h,m}^k
=(I-P_h)u(t)+\big(P_hu(t)-U_{h,m}^k\big).
\]

The first summand is orthogonal to every member of \(V_h\), and the
second belongs to \(V_h\). Therefore Pythagoras gives

\[
\|u(t)-U_{h,m}^k\|^2
=\|(I-P_h)u(t)\|^2+\|P_hu(t)-U_{h,m}^k\|^2.
\]

Using \(u(t)=\sum_jc_j(t)e_j\),
\(U_{h,m}^k=\sum_jb_j^k\phi_{j,h}\), and the orthogonality proved
above, the two terms become

\[
\|(I-P_h)u(t)\|^2=\sum_j(1-g_{j,h})|c_j(t)|^2,
\]

\[
\|P_hu(t)-U_{h,m}^k\|^2
=\sum_jg_{j,h}|c_j(t)-b_j^k|^2.
\]

Thus the exact spatial error is the scalar function

\[
\boxed{
\mathcal F(k,t)=\sum_{j\in\{5,7\}}
\left[g_{j,h}|c_j(t)-b_j^k|^2
+(1-g_{j,h})|c_j(t)|^2\right].}
\]

The weights \(g_{j,h}\) account for the projected basis norms; the
weights \(1-g_{j,h}\) retain the projection residual. This formula
computes the error against the continuum function, including the part of
that function outside \(V_h\). It is not merely a coefficient comparison
within the discrete space.

For example, if all coefficient differences vanished at some time, the
error would still be \(\sum_j(1-g_{j,h})|c_j(t)|^2\). This is exactly
the spatial error of representing \(u(t)\) by its orthogonal projection.

The same decomposition can be written without diagonal Gram matrices.
For any orthonormal continuum family and its projections, let
\(H_{ij}=(P_he_i,P_he_j)\). Then, for real coefficient vectors,

\[
\|u-U\|^2=c^{\mathsf T}(I-H)c+(c-b)^{\mathsf T}H(c-b).
\]

NAP's special setting makes \(H=\operatorname{diag}(g_{5,h},g_{7,h})\)
and also makes the evolution diagonal. The projection decomposition itself
is a general orthogonality identity.

## The exact norm being approximated has not changed

The desired squared norm is

\[
E^2=\int_0^T\|u(t)-U_{h,m}^\tau(t)\|^2\,dt
=\tau\sum_{k=1}^N\int_0^1
\mathcal F\big(k,(k-1+s)\tau\big)\,ds.
\]

This follows by splitting the integral over solver intervals and setting
\(t=(k-1+s)\tau\). The numerical solution is still right-constant,
while \(c_j(t)\) varies continuously inside the interval. Evaluating
only at solver endpoints would give a further quadrature rule for this
same integral.

For matched discrete solutions, \(E_\star\) and NAP's \(\widehat E\)
therefore target the same \(E\). Their finite quadrature values are not
an algebraic identity. NAP has eliminated the reference *spatial*
approximation by using known exact inner products.

# The two time quadratures in NAP

## Gauss--Legendre integration inside each interval

Let \((s_r,w_r)_{r=1}^{Q_t}\) be a Gauss--Legendre rule on \([0,1]\),
with positive weights summing to one. Then

\[
\int_0^1\mathcal F(k,(k-1+s)\tau)\,ds
\approx H(k):=\sum_{r=1}^{Q_t}w_r
\mathcal F(k,(k-1+s_r)\tau).
\]

The rule integrates polynomials of degree at most \(2Q_t-1\) exactly.
The present integrand contains exponentials and trigonometric functions,
so this polynomial exactness does not make the error integral exact.
The default is \(Q_t=4\).

The rule can be constructed from a symmetric Jacobi matrix with zero
diagonal and off-diagonal entries

\[
\frac{r}{\sqrt{4r^2-1}},\qquad r=1,\ldots,Q_t-1.
\]

If its eigenvalues and normalized eigenvectors are \(\eta_r,v_r\),
then transforming the Legendre rule from \([-1,1]\) to \([0,1]\) gives
\(s_r=(\eta_r+1)/2\), \(w_r=(v_r)_1^2\). This explains
`gauss_legendre_rule()` without introducing a new solver time step.

## Recasting the outer sum as an average

Since \(\tau N=T\), after the within-interval quadrature,

\[
E^2\approx \tau\sum_{k=1}^N H(k)
=T\left(\frac1N\sum_{k=1}^NH(k)\right).
\]

The remaining task is to approximate a discrete average over all solver
intervals. Introduce the probability measure

\[
\nu_N=\frac1N\sum_{k=1}^N\delta_{x_k},\qquad
x_k=\frac{k-1/2}{N}.
\]

Then

\[
\frac1N\sum_{k=1}^NH(k)
=\int H(Nx+1/2)\,d\nu_N(x).
\]

This is an integral against a finite discrete measure, which explains why
NAP uses a second Gaussian rule specifically for that measure. A continuous
uniform measure on \([0,1]\) would describe a different average at finite
\(N\).

## Why this particular Jacobi matrix appears

A Gaussian quadrature rule is obtained from orthonormal polynomials for
the chosen measure. Symmetry of \(\nu_N\) about \(1/2\) makes the Jacobi
diagonal equal to \(1/2\).

The off-diagonal can be understood through centered integer coordinates
\(X=k-(N+1)/2\). For monic orthogonal polynomials \(p_\ell(X)\) under
the normalized discrete uniform measure, their squared norms are

\[
h_\ell:=\frac1N\sum_{k=1}^N p_\ell(X_k)^2
=\frac{(\ell!)^4}{(2\ell)!(2\ell+1)!}
\prod_{r=1}^{\ell}(N^2-r^2),\qquad 0\leq\ell<N.
\]

These are the finite-uniform orthogonal-polynomial norm identities; the
empty product for \(\ell=0\) is one. Their ratio is

\[
\frac{h_\ell}{h_{\ell-1}}
=\frac{\ell^2(N^2-\ell^2)}{4(4\ell^2-1)}.
\]

In an orthonormal three-term recurrence the off-diagonal is the square
root of this ratio. Rescaling from \(X\) to \(x=1/2+X/N\) divides it
by \(N\). Thus the normalized Jacobi off-diagonal is

\[
d_\ell=\frac{\ell}{2}
\sqrt{\frac{1-(\ell/N)^2}{4\ell^2-1}}.
\]

For an order \(Q_s\leq N\) rule, diagonalize the \(Q_s\times Q_s\)
Jacobi matrix with this off-diagonal and diagonal \(1/2\). If
\((z_\ell,v_\ell)\) are its normalized eigenpairs, use

\[
W_\ell=(v_\ell)_1^2,\qquad K_\ell=Nz_\ell+1/2.
\]

The weights are positive and sum to one. Gaussian quadrature reproduces
moments through degree \(2Q_s-1\), so

\[
\frac1N\sum_{k=1}^N H(k)
\approx\sum_{\ell=1}^{Q_s}W_\ell H(K_\ell).
\]

If \(Q_s=N\), the rule has the original support and weights, recovering
the finite average exactly. When \(Q_s<N\), it is an approximation.
The code uses \(\min(N,\texttt{step_sum_order})\), normally with requested
order 64, and handles \(N=1\) separately. Its implemented maximum
requested order is 512; recovering an enormous full sum is a mathematical
observation, not the practical acceleration used in the benchmark.

## What noninteger step indices mean

For \(Q_s<N\), the Gaussian indices \(K_\ell\) are usually not integers.
The closed coefficient formula extends to real \(k\) using
\(\mu^k=\exp(k\log\mu)\) and \(e^{ik\theta}\). This defines the
function \(H(k)\) at quadrature nodes while agreeing with the discrete
recurrence at every integer.

There is no claim that a noninteger index is an additional solver iterate.
The analytic extension is used only to approximate the average of the
integer-index values. Different extensions could agree on all integers
and give different reduced quadrature approximations, another reason the
quadrature needs accuracy checks.

Combining both rules gives the reported norm

\[
\boxed{
\widehat E^2=T\sum_{\ell=1}^{Q_s}W_\ell
\sum_{r=1}^{Q_t}w_r
\mathcal F\big(K_\ell,(K_\ell-1+s_r)\tau\big).}
\]

For two modes, \(Q_t=4\), and \(Q_s=64\), this requires two coefficient
values at each of 256 locations. It has no reference spatial dimension
and no loop over \(N\). The factor \(T\) converts the weighted mean
squared error into a time integral; no extra factor \(\tau\) should be
inserted after this normalization.

## What must be checked numerically

Increasing \(Q_t\) tests the within-interval quadrature. Increasing
\(Q_s\) independently tests the approximation of the step average.
These checks serve the role of reference-time refinement in the old
construction, although the rules and approximation errors differ.

For \(N>Q_s\), the implementation rejects cases with

\[
T\max_j\{a_j,\widehat a_j\}>Q_s^2/8
\quad\text{or}\quad |\omega|T>Q_s/2.
\]

This is a resolution guard for strong initial decay or oscillation. It is
not a rigorous quadrature error estimate. The integrand is not polynomial,
so the polynomial exactness of the rule alone cannot justify any claimed
number of accurate digits. `main_copy.tex` reports checks obtained by
doubling the two orders; those measured claims are specific to its stated
data and parameters.

# Stable evaluation of small errors

## Why algebraic equivalence is not sufficient in floating point

The preceding equivalences concern exact mathematical expressions. For
small \(h\), small \(\tau\), and large \(m\), their differences can be
many orders of magnitude smaller than the solution itself. Computing two
accurate order-one quantities and subtracting them can lose the small
error. NAP therefore evaluates several differences algebraically.

Its implementations also use finite Taylor polynomials in small-argument
branches. These are floating-point approximations of the analytic
identities, not additional exact identities. They are intended to make the
truncation negligible in the chosen branches while avoiding cancellation.

## The continuum forcing response

For a general positive rate \(a\),

\[
S_a(t)=A\int_0^t e^{-a(t-s)}\sin(\omega s)\,ds
=A\operatorname{Im}\frac{e^{i\omega t}-e^{-at}}{a+i\omega}.
\]

This is exactly \(e^{-at}G_{\mathrm{sin}}(t)\) from the original
construction. With \(z=(a+i\omega)t\), near zero it can be evaluated as

\[
S_a(t)=Ae^{-at}t\operatorname{Im}
\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^{\infty}\frac{z^\ell}{(\ell+1)!}\right).
\]

The real constant term has no imaginary part and is omitted before
summation. The response begins at \(A\omega t^2/2\); preserving this
small value is the reason for the series. NAP uses 24 terms for
\(|z|<0.5\) and the decayed complex quotient otherwise.

## The spatial projection residual

Directly subtracting \(g_{j,h}\) from one can round a tiny residual to
zero. NAP instead uses a Taylor polynomial beginning with

\[
1-g_{j,h}=\frac{z_j^4}{720}+\frac{z_j^6}{3024}
+\frac{7z_j^8}{259200}+O(z_j^{10}),\qquad z_j=w_jh.
\]

The small-argument branch retains terms through \(z_j^{16}\) when
\(|z_j|<0.1\). This retains the squared spatial error instead of losing
it through subtraction.

## The initial-data coefficient difference

At interval fraction \(s\), put

\[
d=(1-s)\tau,\qquad t=k\tau-d,\qquad
\chi=\tau\widehat a,\qquad \mu=(1+\chi)^{-1}.
\]

Define

\[
H=k\left[\tau(a-\widehat a)+\chi-\log(1+\chi)\right]-ad
=k\log\mu+at.
\]

Then the exponential difference is exactly

\[
I:=e^{-at}-\mu^k
=\begin{cases}
-e^{-at}\operatorname{expm1}(H),&H\leq0,\\
\mu^k\operatorname{expm1}(-H),&H>0.
\end{cases}
\]

Here \(\operatorname{expm1}(x)=e^x-1\), evaluated accurately near zero.
The branch factors out the larger exponential and keeps the `expm1`
argument nonpositive. It avoids an overflowing exponential followed by
multiplication by an underflowing factor.

The other small difference is evaluated through

\[
\chi-\log(1+\chi)=\frac{\chi^2}{2}-\frac{\chi^3}{3}+\cdots.
\]

The implementation uses terms of degrees 2 through 12 for \(\chi<10^{-3}\).
Multiplication by the initial coefficient \(x_j\) then gives the
initial-data contribution to \(c_j(t)-b_j^k\).

## The forcing coefficient difference

Let \(v=\omega\tau/2\). The continuum forcing transfer denominator is

\[
D_e=a+i\omega.
\]

The discrete closed-form denominator can be rewritten using

\[
\frac{e^{i\omega\tau}-\mu}
{\tau\mu\operatorname{sinc}(v)e^{iv}}
=\widehat a\frac{e^{iv}}{\operatorname{sinc}(v)}+i\omega
=:D_n.
\]

Indeed, replacing \(\mu^{-1}\) by \(1+\tau\widehat a\) leaves
\((e^{iv}-e^{-iv})/(\tau\operatorname{sinc}(v))=i\omega\).
With \(\Phi=e^{iv}/\operatorname{sinc}(v)\), write

\[
N_e=e^{i\omega t}-e^{-at},\qquad
N_n=e^{ik\omega\tau}-\mu^k.
\]

The forcing response difference divided by \(Ay_j\) is

\[
\operatorname{Im}\left(\frac{N_e}{D_e}-\frac{N_n}{D_n}\right)
=\operatorname{Im}\left[
\left(\frac1{D_e}-\frac1{D_n}\right)N_n
+\frac{N_e-N_n}{D_e}\right].
\]

Its small factors are available directly:

\[
\frac1{D_e}-\frac1{D_n}
=\frac{-(a-\widehat a)+\widehat a(\Phi-1)}{D_eD_n},
\qquad
N_e-N_n=-e^{i\omega t}(e^{i\omega d}-1)-I.
\]

Near zero,

\[
\Phi-1=v\cot v-1+iv
=-\frac{v^2}{3}-\frac{v^4}{45}-\frac{2v^6}{945}
-\frac{v^8}{4725}-\frac{2v^{10}}{93555}+O(v^{12})+iv.
\]

Phase increments use
\(e^{i\eta}-1=-2\sin^2(\eta/2)+i\sin\eta\), and powers use
\(\mu^k=\exp[-k\operatorname{log1p}(\tau\widehat a)]\).
These rearrangements explain `uniform_modal_difference()`. When
\(|\omega\tau|\geq0.1\), it instead subtracts the literal continuum
and numerical coefficient arrays. The present studies use the small-step
branch.

# A different coefficient source is a genuine change of input

## What the two repositories select

The derivation of the matrix-to-scalar equivalence works for any fixed
admissible rational function \(\mathcal R\). The shipped repositories
select that function differently.

NAFDEMG-main reads `rSPDE` tables for \(m=1,2,3,4\). For a requested
\(\beta\), it linearly interpolates each root and the factor between
table rows. Denote the resulting function by
\(\mathcal R_{m,\beta}^{\mathrm{pkg}}\).

NAP's convergence wrapper selects computed coefficients generated directly
at

\[
m=1,\ldots,8,\qquad \beta\in\{0.25,0.45,0.65\},\qquad
\delta_m=10^{-(5+m)/2}.
\]

For each pair, Cheb--Padé approximation was applied to
\(x^{\beta-1}\) on \([\delta_m,1]\), with numerator degree \(m\)
and denominator degree \(m+1\). The root/factor artifact stores 17
significant digits. Denote its function by
\(\mathcal R_{m,\beta}^{\mathrm{cmp}}\).

NAP selects stored beta values within a floating-point equality tolerance;
it does not interpolate between them. Order eight has a separately
generated coefficient set, and is not extrapolated from orders 1--4.
MATLAB generation precedes the notebook runs.

The two rational functions may agree at some parameter choices, but equality
does not follow from matching \((m,\beta)\). If
\(\mathcal R^{\mathrm{pkg}}(z_j)\ne\mathcal R^{\mathrm{cmp}}(z_j)\),
then their decay rates and backward Euler multipliers differ. This changes
the discrete evolution itself, independently of whether it is evaluated
by sparse solves or by modal formulas.

The NAP selector retains a package-source option, but
`tadpole_convergence_error()` explicitly chooses the computed source. An
equivalence check must deliberately supply the same coefficients to both
forms of the scheme.

## What root validation proves

The computed path checks the root counts, a finite positive factor,
finite real negative roots, and strict interlacing. In increasing order,
the roots satisfy

\[
\zeta_1<\xi_1<\zeta_2<\cdots<\xi_m<\zeta_{m+1}<0.
\]

For \(z>0\), each linear factor \(1-\xi_i z\) and
\(1-\zeta_i z\) is positive. This establishes positivity of the
rational inverse and of its decay rates. Interlacing is an additional
structural admissibility check.

These conditions do not establish an approximation error bound for
\(\mathcal R(z)-z^{-\beta}\). They also do not establish best uniform
rational approximation or accurate evaluation on every fine-mesh mode.

For example, on a selected mode, if

\[
\mathcal R(z_j)=z_j^{-\beta}(1+\varepsilon_j),\qquad
|\varepsilon_j|\leq\eta<1,
\]

then

\[
\frac{\widehat a_j}{a_{j,h}}=\frac1{1+\varepsilon_j},\qquad
\left|\frac{\widehat a_j}{a_{j,h}}-1\right|
\leq\frac{\eta}{1-\eta}.
\]

This is a quantitative rate-error statement if the relative approximation
error is known. Root negativity alone supplies no such value of \(\eta\).

## Active-mode accuracy and full-spectrum interval coverage

The normalized reciprocal spectrum is

\[
\sigma(B^{-1})\subset
[\delta_h,1],\qquad
\delta_h=\frac{\kappa^2}{\lambda_{\max,h}}.
\]

To apply an approximation guarantee on a generation interval
\([\delta,1]\) to the entire operator, that interval must contain the
whole reciprocal spectrum. In particular, \(\delta\leq\delta_h\) is
required. Appropriate approximation error bounds on that interval are
also required; coverage alone is not sufficient.

The distinction is concrete for the present mesh. Its loop has \(2n\)
elements, so an alternating nodal vector is consistent around the loop
and along the terminal edge. On every element it has opposite endpoint
values. The stiffness/mass ratio for an element with endpoint values
\(a,b\) is

\[
\frac{(a-b)^2/h}{h(a^2+ab+b^2)/3}\leq\frac{12}{h^2},
\]

with equality when \(a=-b\). Hence the global alternating vector attains
the upper Rayleigh bound, and

\[
\lambda_{\max,h}=\kappa^2+12h^{-2}.
\]

At \(\kappa=4\) and \(h=10^{-5}\),

\[
\delta_h=\frac{16}{16+12\times10^{10}}
\approx1.33\times10^{-10},\qquad
\delta_8=10^{-6.5}\approx3.16\times10^{-7}.
\]

Thus the order-eight generation interval does **not** cover the full
reciprocal spectrum on that mesh. A uniform operator error theorem based
on complete interval coverage cannot be certified by these fixed-interval
coefficient checks alone.

By contrast, the two active reciprocal eigenvalues, for fine meshes, are
approximately

\[
\frac{16}{16+(3\pi/2)^2}\approx0.42,\qquad
\frac{16}{16+(2\pi)^2}\approx0.29.
\]

Their actual FEM counterparts remain well within the generation intervals
throughout the stated experiments. Only these two values affect the
exact-load solution, because the other modes are unexcited. This explains
the finite-mode scope stated in `main_copy.tex`.

There are two separate assertions: the modal evaluation is exactly the
restriction of the chosen rational matrix scheme, and the chosen rational
scheme approximates the desired fractional operator accurately. The first
was proved above. The second requires approximation estimates or numerical
accuracy evidence on the relevant spectrum. Computational equivalence
does not supply that evidence automatically.

# What the convergence studies now test

## Spatial and temporal reference slopes

For the theoretical scheme under its approximation hypotheses, the error
estimate has the form

\[
E\lesssim \tau+h^{\min\{\alpha+2s,2\}-\epsilon}
+h^{\alpha-2}\exp(-c_\alpha\sqrt m),\qquad
c_\alpha=2\pi\sqrt{1-\alpha/2},
\]

where \(s\in[0,1]\) describes data regularity and \(\epsilon>0\) is
sufficiently small. The finite eigenfunction data belong to every
nonnegative spectral Sobolev space, so the spatial prediction saturates
at \(2-\epsilon\). NAP uses the limiting reference slope 2.

This is also visible directly in the modal construction. For fixed active
wave numbers,

\[
\lambda_{j,h}-\lambda_j=O(h^2),\qquad
a_{j,h}-a_j=O(h^2),\qquad
\|e_j-P_he_j\|=O(h^2).
\]

Smooth dependence of the finite set of scalar solutions on their rates
then gives second-order spatial behavior when auxiliary errors are small.
This does not conflict with the weaker \(h^{\alpha-\epsilon}\) estimate
obtained by using less of the available data regularity.

For fixed positive rate \(a\),

\[
\log\mu=-\log(1+\tau a)
=-\tau a+\frac{\tau^2a^2}{2}+O(\tau^3).
\]

For fixed \(t=k\tau\), the accumulated exponent error is \(O(\tau)\).
The right-constant reconstruction also introduces a within-interval
\(O(\tau)\) difference for these smooth solutions. Thus NAP retains the
first-order temporal reference slope 1.

The analytic loss \(\epsilon\) is distinct from machine precision and
from the roundoff tolerances used to identify grid values. NAP does not
introduce a numerical experiment parameter \(\epsilon\) to generate its
reference slope.

## Why the rational slope is a benchmark

The rational part of the bound suggests the scale

\[
\log E\sim-c_\alpha\sqrt m+\text{constant}
\]

only as a comparison of decay scales. An upper bound does not imply
equality, asymptotic sharpness, or a straight line over \(m=1,2,3,4\).
The computed approximants also have order-dependent generation intervals,
and the experiment samples only two smooth modes.

Both constructions fit a regression against \(\sqrt m\). NAP labels
\(-c_\alpha\) as a bound benchmark and does not attach a percentage
agreement error between that benchmark and the fitted rational slope.
It retains slope-percentage comparisons for the spatial and temporal
reference lines. The fitted relations are

\[
\log E=s_h\log h+b_h,\qquad
\log E=s_\tau\log\tau+b_\tau,\qquad
\ln E=s_m\sqrt m+b_m.
\]

The first two slopes are unchanged if the logarithm base is changed on
both axes. The rational slope uses the natural logarithm specifically.
Guide curves have prescribed slopes and data-dependent vertical placement;
their heights are not rigorous upper-bound constants.

## The diagnostic with exact discrete fractional rates

NAP's `m = 0` flag bypasses rational coefficients and uses

\[
\widehat a_j=a_{j,h}=\lambda_{j,h}^\beta.
\]

It still uses \(P_he_j\), the same FEM eigenvalues, backward Euler,
right-constant reconstruction, and the same error quadrature. The
resulting \(E_{\mathrm{st}}\) measures the combined spatial/time error
with rational approximation removed. It is not a zeroth-order rational
approximant. At \(\alpha=2\), exact discrete rates are also used
regardless of \(m\).

The spatial projection residual and projected coefficient error have an
orthogonal squared-error decomposition. The temporal and rational parts
of the coefficient error generally do not: they can reinforce or cancel.
Thus subtracting \(E_{\mathrm{st}}\) from the total error does not isolate
a rational error norm.

If \(U_R\) and \(U_{\mathrm{st}}\) denote the two reconstructed numerical
solutions, the reverse triangle inequality only gives

\[
\left|\|u-U_R\|-\|u-U_{\mathrm{st}}\|\right|
\leq\|U_R-U_{\mathrm{st}}\|.
\]

Ratios and parameter-halving comparisons therefore provide sensitivity
checks for this experiment. They are not a general certified a posteriori
estimator. The quadrature-doubling and auxiliary-parameter checks reported
in `main_copy.tex` must be understood in that sense.

# Changes to the actual experiments and to their descriptions

## Current notebook settings

The following table compares the configured NAFDEMG-main notebooks with
NAP's shared parameters. The same graph and amplitudes are used throughout,
with \(\kappa=4\) and \(\alpha\in\{0.5,0.9,1.3\}\).

| Setting | NAFDEMG-main notebooks | NAP / `main_copy.tex` |
|---|---|---|
| Final time | \(10^{-3}\) | \(1\) |
| Spatial study: requested sizes | Four targets from \(9\times10^{-4}\) to \(10^{-2}\) | Six targets from \(10^{-4}\) to \(10^{-2}\) |
| Spatial study: fixed values | Target \(\tau=10^{-9}\), \(m=4\) | \(\tau=10^{-10}\), \(m=8\) |
| Temporal study: requested steps | Four targets from \(9\times10^{-6}\) to \(10^{-4}\) | Six targets from \(10^{-4}\) to \(10^{-2}\) |
| Temporal study: fixed values | Spatial target \(h=10^{-4}\), \(m=4\) | \(h=10^{-5}\), \(m=8\) |
| Rational study | \(m=1,2,3,4\), spatial target \(h=10^{-4}\), target \(\tau=5\times10^{-9}\) | \(m=1,2,3,4\), \(h=10^{-5}\), \(\tau=10^{-10}\) |
| Spatial-study reference grid | \(h_\star=5\times10^{-5}\), target \(\tau_\star=2\times10^{-10}\) | Analytic spatial error, two time quadratures |
| Temporal/rational reference grid | \(h_\star=9\times10^{-5}\), target \(\tau_\star=10^{-9}\) | Analytic spatial error, two time quadratures |
| Rational source | Package tables, orders 1--4 | Computed exact-beta coefficients, orders 1--8 |

For a requested time step \(\eta\), both workflows construct an actual
uniform grid with

\[
N=\lceil T/\eta\rceil,\qquad \tau=T/N.
\]

NAP includes a near-integer roundoff snap, retains only the scalar grid
description, and limits supported exact step indices. The original helper
also constructs the complete time vector. NAP's actual spatial sizes are
\(h=1/\lceil\eta^{-1}\rceil\), and its regressions use the actual
spatial and temporal values.

Increasing \(T\) changes the integration interval, the decay history,
and the part of the sine forcing sampled by the experiment. It is not a
change that can generally be corrected by multiplying the old error by
\(\sqrt{T_{\mathrm{new}}/T_{\mathrm{old}}}\).

The old `N_finite = 4` and NAP's value 4 both generate the wave-number
catalogue \((0,1,2,2,3,4,4)\). Indices 5 and 7 select the active modes.
This value is not the finite element dimension, rational order, or a
truncation of a nonzero infinite spectral tail.

## `main.tex` and the current old notebooks are not identical snapshots

The numerical-experiments prose in `main.tex` lists some values different
from its current corresponding notebooks. This is a documentation issue
separate from the mathematical equivalence proved above:

* It lists alpha values \(1.0,1.2,1.4,1.6,1.8\), whereas the inspected
  notebooks use \(0.5,0.9,1.3\).
* It describes six spatial and temporal refinement values, whereas the
  current notebooks use four in each study.
* It lists temporal targets from \(9\times10^{-4}\) to \(10^{-2}\),
  whereas the temporal notebook uses \(9\times10^{-6}\) to \(10^{-4}\).
  With its stated \(T=10^{-3}\), most targets in the prose exceed the
  final time and produce only one solver interval; they cannot generate
  the intended distinct six-point temporal study under the grid rule above.
* It lists one reference grid for all studies. The inspected spatial
  notebook uses that grid, while the temporal and rational notebooks use
  the reference values in the preceding table.
* Its smooth-data discussion gives the saturated spatial prediction
  \(2-\epsilon\), but the figure caption and original spatial plot use
  \(\alpha-\epsilon\) or \(\alpha\). NAP uses slope 2 consistently.

Consequently there are three snapshots to distinguish: the old manuscript
description, the current old notebook settings, and the new NAP settings.
The results and percentage claims in the old manuscript cannot be carried
over to NAP by an algebraic change of representation.

# An explicit statement of what is and is not equivalent

**Proposition.** Fix a uniform tadpole mesh of common element length
\(h=1/n\), the consistent P1 mass inner product, \(\kappa>0\),
\(0<\alpha\leq2\), a uniform time grid, and the same positive rational
inverse \(\mathcal R\) when \(\alpha<2\). Use the same physical modal
data and exact spatial loads. Suppose the selected modes are resolved as
above. Then:

1. The original shifted matrix update and the scalar recurrence define
   the same finite element iterate \(U_{h,m}^k\) for every integer \(k\).
2. The closed coefficient formula evaluates those iterates exactly as an
   algebraic expression.
3. The scalar expression \(\mathcal F(k,t)\) equals their full spatial
   squared error against the continuum solution.
4. Integrating \(\mathcal F\) exactly gives the same target space--time
   error norm as the matrix/reference construction is intended to measure.

The proof consists of the generalized eigenvalue identity, projection
identity, invariant-subspace induction, finite geometric sum, and
orthogonal error decomposition derived in this note. No reference-space
limit is used to prove the discrete evolution identity.

The two reported errors at finite quadrature resolution satisfy a different
kind of comparison. If the physical problem and final time have first been
matched, let \(E_{\mathrm{NAP}}\) and \(E_{\mathrm{main}}\) denote the
exact norms for their respective numerical solutions. Then

\[
\widehat E_{\mathrm{NAP}}-E_{\star,\mathrm{main}}
=(\widehat E_{\mathrm{NAP}}-E_{\mathrm{NAP}})
+(E_{\mathrm{NAP}}-E_{\mathrm{main}})
+(E_{\mathrm{main}}-E_{\star,\mathrm{main}}).
\]

The first and last terms are error-measurement discrepancies. The middle
term is a discrepancy between discrete solutions and obeys

\[
|E_{\mathrm{NAP}}-E_{\mathrm{main}}|
\leq\|U_{\mathrm{NAP}}^\tau-U_{\mathrm{main}}^\tau\|_{L_2(0,T;L_2(\Gamma))}.
\]

Matching mesh, coefficients, loads, and time grid makes this middle term
zero. Matching the time horizon alone, or matching only the rational order
\(m\), does not. The remaining terms must be controlled by their own
quadrature/refinement checks.

For a numerical comparison of the two evaluation methods, first match the
actual partition, \(T\), \(\tau\), \(\alpha\), all root/factor entries,
and the exact loads. Compare the finite element states at integer solver
times. Only after establishing that equality should the two error
quadratures be compared. This separates evolution equivalence from
measurement accuracy and from the changed scientific experiment.

# Source guide and notation-to-code dictionary

The derivations above are self-contained. These links identify where the
mathematical objects occur in the inspected sources; they are not needed
to supply missing equations.

| Mathematical object or operation | NAFDEMG-main | NAP |
|---|---|---|
| Graph, continuum modes, and eigenvalue ordering | `gets.graph.tadpole()`, `tadpole.eig()`, `gets.eigen.params()` | Wave-number catalogue in `uniform_tadpole_basis()` |
| \(P_h(10e_5)\) | `project_u0_tadpole()` | Initial coefficient 10 multiplying \(\phi_{5,h}\) |
| \(\lambda_{j,h}\), \(g_{j,h}\), \(1-g_{j,h}\) | Implicit in FEM matrices and reference comparisons | `discrete_eigenvalues`, diagonal of `gram`, diagonal of `residual_gram` |
| Scalar rational inverse | Package `my.get.roots()` and polynomial update construction | `my.get.roots()` and product in `rational_modal_rates()` |
| \(\widehat a_j\), \(\mu_j\) | Implicit in the shifted solves | Returned rates and `exp(logq)` |
| Averaged sine forcing | `average_sine_forcing()` | Sinc factor in the closed recurrence |
| Integer-step evolution | `my.solver.frac()` inside `solve_fractional_evolution_error()` | `uniform_modal_coefficients()`; stable difference on the error path |
| \(c_j(t)\) | `G_sin()` multiplied by the decaying exponential | `exact_modal_coefficients()` and `decayed_sine_convolution()` |
| \(c_j(t)-b_j^k\) | Implicit after reference-space evaluation | `uniform_modal_difference()` |
| Spatial squared error | `error` and `reference_C` quadratic form | `squared` from modal Gram and residual terms |
| Time integration of error | Reference times and endpoint weights | `gauss_legendre_rule()`, `discrete_uniform_rule()` |
| Reported norm | `solve_fractional_evolution_error()` | `uniform_tadpole_error()`, called by `tadpole_convergence_error()` |
